name: dnstwist
desc: Test domains for typo squatting, phishing and corporate espionage
why: Generates typosquatted domain variants and resolves them, a window into DNS and how phishing domains get found.

brief.what_it_is: dnstwist is a Python command-line tool that takes a domain name and generates lookalike variants of it using several fuzzing algorithms (homoglyph, hyphenation, and others), plus optional dictionary words and TLDs. By default it then does DNS lookups on each variant and reports which ones resolve, along with their DNS records. Output goes to the terminal, CSV, or JSON, or can be limited to bare permutations with no lookups. Optional modes fetch each live site and compare its HTML fuzzy hash (ssdeep or TLSH) or headless-Chromium screenshot pHash against the original, and can add GeoIP country and rogue MX detection.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to "See what sort of trouble users can get in trying to type your domain name" and to "Find lookalike domains that adversaries can use to attack you." It is meant as a source of targeted threat intelligence for defenders such as SOC and incident response teams.
brief.how_it_works: It permutes the input domain with its fuzzers, then resolves each permutation to see whether it is registered. With --lsh it fetches the HTTP content of resolving domains, normalizes the HTML, and compares a fuzzy hash to the original site's hash as a similarity percentage. With --phash it uses headless Chromium to take screenshots and compares perceptual hashes. The README also notes that the homoglyph fuzzer is built from Unicode characters that can actually be registered.

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install, the README lists pip install dnstwist[full] (with all extras) or bare pip install dnstwist plus manual extras, a git clone and pip install . route, sudo apt install dnstwist (Debian/Ubuntu/Kali), sudo dnf install dnstwist (Fedora), yay -S dnstwist (Arch AUR), and Docker. For GeoIP, the GeoIP2 library is used by default, and the country database path must be set in the $GEOLITE2_MMDB environment variable; otherwise it falls back to the older GeoIP Legacy. Proxies are picked up from standard <scheme>_proxy environment variables. The --phash mode needs Chromium installed. Heavy runs may need an external resolver via --nameservers, including DNS-over-HTTPS.
brief.standout: Most lookalike-domain tools stop at listing permutations. This one adds a phishing-page check, comparing fuzzy HTML hashes and screenshot perceptual hashes against the original site. It is also built to be used as a library, with a dnstwist.run() API that returns a list of dictionaries.
brief.status: Unknown from the material I read. The GitHub page I got back shows the README with no release date or last-commit date, and the README has no maintenance note. Signs of an active project: multiple package routes (PyPI, apt, dnf, AUR, Homebrew, Docker Hub) and a long list of security-vendor integrations. I did not verify a recent commit or release.
brief.caveats: Heavy use can overwhelm DNS resolvers, and the README advises a fast external resolver for large runs. --phash needs a full Chromium install and substantial free memory because of its multithreaded browser use. GeoIP needs a separate MaxMind-style database file. The README says coverage is deliberately limited to likely permutations and that exhaustive checking is impractical for long domains. It also says a 100% HTML hash match is unlikely even in MITM kits, and that a phishing site can have completely different HTML. The README does not discuss legal or ethical limits on probing or fetching third-party domains. The homepage text I got showed only a Scan box and a source link, and I did not test that web interface.

entry.title: dnstwist
entry.tldr: Give it a domain and it generates lookalike typo and homoglyph variants, then checks which ones are actually registered and what they serve.
entry.deeper_look:
dnstwist takes a domain name and runs it through a set of fuzzing algorithms: homoglyphs, hyphenation, and others. It can also add words from a dictionary file. Each permutation is then resolved over DNS to see whether someone has registered it, and the records come back in the terminal, as CSV, or as JSON. A passive mode skips the lookups and just prints the permutations.

The README frames the purpose as seeing "what sort of trouble users can get in trying to type your domain name". It is built for defenders, such as SOC and incident response teams, who want to find lookalike domains before an attacker uses them. The homoglyph fuzzer draws on Unicode characters that can actually be registered, so the list reflects what an attacker could really buy.

Two optional modes go past DNS. With `--lsh`, it fetches each live page, normalizes the HTML, and compares a fuzzy hash against the original site, reporting a similarity percentage. With `--phash`, it takes headless Chromium screenshots and compares perceptual hashes. Both are attempts to tell a parked domain from a copied login page.

Underneath is a good way into how DNS, internationalized domain names, and phishing infrastructure fit together. You see how easily one name fans out into hundreds of near-neighbors, and how few of them need to resolve to cause trouble. It also works as a Python library through `dnstwist.run()`, which returns a list of dictionaries.
entry.install:
brew install dnstwist
# Optional: --phash needs Chromium installed; GeoIP needs a MaxMind-style database with its path in $GEOLITE2_MMDB

try_this.what_happens: Prints the bare permutations with no DNS lookups, so you can see what the fuzzers produce without touching anyone's servers.
Runs the fuzzers, resolves each variant, and shows only the ones that are registered.
Limits generation to the named algorithms, which makes it easy to compare what each one contributes.

entry.whats_unique: Most lookalike-domain tools stop at listing permutations. This one also fetches the live pages and compares fuzzy HTML hashes and screenshot perceptual hashes against the original site.
entry.caveats: Large runs can overwhelm your DNS resolver, so the README advises a fast external one, and `--phash` needs a full Chromium install and a lot of memory.
